TIER 1 PROCESS SAFETY EVENTS (PSE)
Tier 1 PSE are predominantly lagging indicators related to Loss of Primary Containment (LOPC) referred to as a 
Process Safety Event (PSE). The Tier 1 Key Performance Indicator (KPI) records events with greater consequence 
within the four-tier approach.
For more information see IOGP Report 456 - Process Safety – recommended practice on key performance indicators. 
IOGP has been gathering Tier 1 PSE narrative reports from its Members since 2013. These include Tier 1 PSE 
reported both by companies and contractors. Event reports are categorized by region, country, location (onshore/
offshore), cause, activity at the time of the event, and, from 2019 onwards, point of release.
The information provided here is not detailed; often the root cause of an incident cannot be established. However, 
the information should assist organizations to identify likely hazards and to question whether their own Safety 
Management System would have prevented the event occurring and mitigated its consequences.
The database from 2020 onwards is available and searchable at https://data.iogp.org/ProcessSafety/Tier1PSE. 
Note that a descriptive report has not been provided for every Tier 1 PSE reported.
This database is a tool for learning and should not be considered a complete record of Tier 1 PSE in the 
upstream oil and gas industry or the IOGP Membership.

DATE: 27 Jul 2025
COUNTRY: Angola

ACTIVITY: Unspecified - other
MODE OF OPERATION: Normal
POINT OF RELEASE:  Subsea: Subsea pipeline/flowline
PROCESS SAFETY FUNDAMENTAL:  Not applicable.
INCIDENT DESCRIPTION:
At approximately 11:50 AM, a gas release was observed in the vicinity. The incident was reported by the surfer boat 
Captain who observed visible gas bubbles breaking the sea surface along the pipelines route. 
Subsea team started a sonar survey to locate any abnormalities on the gas lines in the area. The Subsea team 
widened the survey area and focused on 8” gas line and detected a gas release from this line which was confirmed 
to be the source of the observed bubbling.
WHAT WENT WRONG?
Subsea gas leak was discovered after survey.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS & RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. Area superintendent should form a cross-functional team to assess practicality and cost-effectiveness and 
prioritize repairs or process adjustments, including reinstating pigging capabilities and implementing alternative 
integrity assessment methods such as hydro testing and internal and external corrosion direct assessment - ICDA 
and ECDA, in line with company guidelines. Sept 30th, 2026. 
2. Area superintendent to engage and set clear expectations to Operations frontline leaders and preservation 
coordinator to strictly follow and meet the requirements of the existing Fixed Equipment Inventory Guideline and 
preservation procedures. These documents are held by preservation team.
• Involve operations and preservation coordinator to develop the preservation protocol for the identified equipment 
and ensure proper MOC is documented for the equipment placed out of service. 
• Consider involving Process Safety, Reliability, and Integrity - HCEPO (High Consequence Equipment Program 
Owner) positions in the communication of any change in equipment status. 
• Consider involving chemical SME on chemical requirements for preservation. Mar 31st, 2026.
3. Chemical specialist should verify that chemical treatment deficiencies are addressed through the new contract, 
ensuring products match fluid characteristics, and consider multiple contracts to overcome current supplier 
limitations. Due date: Mar 31st, 2026. 
4. Asset integrity pipelines & corrosion team lead to develop Inspection, testing preventive maintenance (ITPMs) for 
piggable and unpiggable pipelines, and dashboards for tracking and monitoring the KPIs from the fluid sampling 
and corrosion monitoring information. ITPM should define:

DATE: 04 Sep 2025
COUNTRY: Angola
FUNCTION: Production
NUMBER OF DEATHS: 0
ACTIVITY: Production operations
MODE OF OPERATION: Normal
POINT OF RELEASE:  Relief, Vent and Discharge Systems: Flare and atmospheric vent systems (intended discharge 
location)
PROCESS SAFETY FUNDAMENTAL:  We recognize change.
INCIDENT DESCRIPTION:
On 04 September 2025, an uncontrolled release of approximately 1,064 kg of hydrocarbon and inert gas mixture 
occurred from the cargo tank vent lines on an FPSO, resulting in Emergency Shutdown activation. The release was 
caused by valves 64HCV0001 and 64HCV0002 opening unexpectedly during a reboot of controller.
WHAT WENT WRONG?
Controller failure was due to a firmware bug.
No formal agreement with supplier on timelines for firmware fixes or release notes during commissioning.
A software backup was performed during cold venting activities without prior communication between the ICSS FSR 
and the operations team. Additionally, the ICSS FSR did not verify the card restart configuration before generating 
and uploading the backup. The controller’s configuration module was set to return to its “last saved” value upon 
restart when redundancy was not available.
Daily check for monitoring overall controller status was not established at this stage (Commissioning + Operation).
CROs not focus on system alarms at this stage (Commissioning + Operation).
Onboard team relied on verbal risk assessment. MOC “Deviation” exists, but triggers unclear for abnormal 
conditions.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS & RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Complete the firmware upgrade on the controllers.
• Develop and formalize a clear process that defines timelines and responsibilities for execution of anomalies 
and/or safety alerts.
• Conduct a comprehensive review of all controller module parameter configurations to confirm the safest restart 
settings are applied.
• Establish procedure to manage software changes during commissioning.
• For future projects, in alignment with the established process philosophy and specifically for systems that may 
result in unintended hydrocarbon releases to the atmosphere, it is essential to verify and define the software 
configurations during the engineering phase. These settings should ensure that actuated valves assume the 
safest possible position during restart conditions.
• Develop and implement a daily controller status verification checklist for the DCS Technician detailing specific 
items to check, timing, and completion steps.
• Improve and develop prioritization of the alarms for supporting control room operators’ activities.

PROCESS SAFETY FUNDAMENTAL:  Not applicable.
INCIDENT DESCRIPTION:
At approximately 0523 hrs. on November 8, 2025, an unusual sound was observed at the facility. Upon investigation, 
operations identified a fire on the upper section of the Auto-Thermal Reformer Unit 1 (ATR1). The Emergency 
Response Team (ERT) was immediately deployed to the location. In accordance with the plant’s safety and control 
systems, ATR Units 1 and 2 as well as ASU Units 1 and 2 underwent automatic shutdowns due to inter-unit 
protective logic. The fire was fully extinguished by approximately 0630 hrs. There was no injury to personnel.
WHAT WENT WRONG?
Operating limits and equipment reliability.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS & RECOMMENDATIONS:
IR cameras previously installed had no capability for tracking and alerting operations of temperature changes.
The Isolation valve between reforming section and cooling train opened on loss of instrument air, contrary to its 
Fail-Last-Open (FLO) design intent. Latent functional defects went undetected due to the absence of a robust fail-
safe validation program.

DATE: 23 Sep 2025
COUNTRY: Bangladesh
FUNCTION: Production
NUMBER OF DEATHS: 0
ACTIVITY: Unspecified - other
MODE OF OPERATION: Normal
POINT OF RELEASE:  Onshore Pipelines/Flowlines: Onshore pipeline
PROCESS SAFETY FUNDAMENTAL:  We sustain barriers.
INCIDENT DESCRIPTION:
23 Sep 2025, 2:58 AM: Pressure drop (~6 psi) was detected during condensate shipping. Operations halted and 
security alerted.
Early Response: 
BY Security Control Room (BYSCR) coordinated with Quick Response Team (QRT), local police, and pipeline officer. 
Foot patrols conducted (6:00–9:45 AM). No abnormality observed; shipping resumed at 11:50 AM after GTCL 
confirmation.
Community Alert & Spill Confirmation (5:15–5:37 PM): 
Community reported condensate smell: shipping stopped. QRT confirmed spill at site.
Escalation: 
5:38 PM: Incident Management Team (IMT) activated; Emergency Response Team (ERT 1) formed at 6:20 PM.
7:04 PM: Significant spill spread to low-lying land and canal waterways. ERT 1 left the necessary preparation, tools/ 
logistics, for incident site at 7:30 pm (2-hour journey).
9:05 PM: Fire breakout reported; ERT 1 diverted to extinguish fire at bridge.
9:10 PM: Fire Service & Civil Defense (FSCD) engaged; fire extinguished by 10:20 PM with joint effort.
Leak Source & Containment:
11:55 PM: Leak source identified (illegal tapping with ball valve); area blocked with heavy soil. 
24 Sep, 12:55 PM: The area was secured, and containment measures were implemented. Eventually, the leak was 
plugged, and 22. bbl condensate was recovered. Approximately 173 bbl condensate spill occurred.
Third party injuries: 
Media reported three community members critically burned during the fire: hospitalized. 
Tragically, three members of a nearby community, despite intensive care, passed away (two on 28 Sep, one on 1 
Oct). The incident resulted in environmental contamination, property damage, and third-party loss of life.
WHAT WENT WRONG?
Illegal tap.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS & RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. Inadequate engineering safeguard to prevent pipeline intrusion 
• No current effective technological means in place for pipeline surveillance.
2. Ineffective security patrolling 
• Security patrolling did not detect any abnormalities across pipeline ROW during/before illegal tap or after control 
room detection of potential concern via observed condensate pipeline pressure drop with increased flow rate.
3. Illegal tap leading to LOC escalating up to fire and impacting community personnel was not adequately anticipated

the community, leading to delayed risk mitigation and continued exposure to condensate and ignition hazards.

INCIDENT DESCRIPTION:
Fatal fire following premature restart during PSV maintenance.
WHAT WENT WRONG?
A premature restart of the system without verifying reinstatement of the PSV resulted in uncontrolled hydrocarbon 
release, gas accumulation, ignition from a modified adjacent burner opening, and a fatal fire incident.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS & RECOMMENDATIONS:
Critical safety devices must never be removed or bypassed without ensuring positive mechanical isolation, 
structured restart control, and thorough hazard assessment, particularly in hydrocarbon environments with 
adjacent operating units.

fluids downhole.
• Accuracy and completeness of cessation of production records are essential to inform decommissioning risks 
and execution methodology.

INCIDENT DESCRIPTION:
During a walkthrough on the platform, a worker who was holding the position of Helper C perceived an abnormal 
noise near the fuel gas regulation package, which operates at 74 kg/cm². Upon inspecting the package, he identified 
the presence of gas in a 2” Ø x 600# line located on the mezzanine of the first level.
As he inspected the line more closely, he detected a loss of containment at the threaded connection between the 2” 
Ø x 600# line and the 2” x 600# coupling. He proceeded to tighten the 2” Ø coupling to the 2” Ø pipe, observing that 
the gas emission gradually decreased. Immediately afterward, the threaded coupling detached, leaving his left palm 
exposed to the gas coming out of the pipe.
He immediately informed the Control Room and secured the residual gas system. With support from the first aid 
brigade of the Processing Centre, he was transferred, conscious and walking on his own, from platform to the 
Processing Centre via lateral flight for medical attention.
WHAT WENT WRONG?
A loss of containment occurred at a threaded connection on a high-pressure fuel gas line (˜74 kg/cm²).
The worker attempted to tighten a leaking threaded coupling while the line was pressurized, which is unsafe.
Tightening the live connection caused the threaded coupling to fail and detach completely, exposing the worker’s 
hand directly to escaping gas.
Threaded fittings are not robust for high-pressure gas service and are prone to failure due to vibration, wear, 
misalignment, or improper makeup.
Immediate isolation and depressurization were not performed before intervention, increasing the risk of injury and 
escalation.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS & RECOMMENDATIONS:
Never tighten or repair a leaking pressurized gas connection. Any gas leak must trigger stop work, evacuation, 
notification to the Control Room, isolation, and depressurization.
Threaded connections should be avoided in high-pressure fuel gas systems; welded or flanged joints are safer and 
more reliable.

INCIDENT DESCRIPTION:
On March 7th, 2025, the platform experienced a major process safety incident when the hinge pin of the dome 
on a Cargo Tank starboard catastrophically failed. The rupture of the hinge pin resulted in the complete loss of 
mechanical restraint of the dome, causing the dome cover to fully open and exposing the entire tank opening to 
atmosphere. This structural failure led to the uncontrolled release of a flammable gas mixture directly onto the deck.
The plant’s gas detection system was activated, initiating an emergency shutdown (ESD). Personnel were mustered 
in the accommodation module; however, a continuous flammable gas cloud was extending laterally across the full 
width of the platform, spanning from one side to the other. As a result, access to the muster location necessarily 
required personnel to pass through the flammable gas cloud.
The tanks were depressurized both through the fully open dome, which was already providing an unrestricted 
release path, and by remotely opening the vent stacks. Despite these depressurization measures, the uncontrolled 
release continued for nearly one hour, until the tanks were fully vented and pressure equalized with the atmosphere.
Fortunately, there were no injuries, fires, explosions, or environmental impacts. Nevertheless, production was 
halted, and personnel were exposed to significant risk due to the prolonged presence of a flammable atmosphere 
across the installation.
WHAT WENT WRONG?
The root cause investigation identified that the main threat was progressive corrosion on the dome’s hinge pin, 
caused by an inadequate weld that was smaller than specified in the original design. Weaknesses in the preventive 
safety barriers allowed this defect to persist: the inspection plan did not require detailed checks on the dome pin, 
and a maintenance anomaly had been incorrectly reported in the system (as a generic defect note instead of a 
specific inspection note, and linked to a general location instead of the dome pin). These failures in inspection and 
anomaly management meant the integrity problem was neither prioritized nor properly addressed, allowing the 
degradation to continue unnoticed until catastrophic failure.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS & RECOMMENDATIONS:
The incident highlighted the need for robust inspection and maintenance protocols focused on critical structural 
joints of tank covers. Inspections must be properly planned and rigorously executed to verify weld quality, 
dimensional compliance, and integrity at hinge assemblies, pivot points, and attachment areas. Maintenance 
reporting processes should require precise classification and direct linkage of each finding to the exact component 
affected, avoiding generic location references. Information management systems must include all relevant 
structural elements to prevent misregistration or omission of critical observations.
Design and procurement standards should mandate verification of structural joints and weld integrity at 
commissioning and throughout the operational lifecycle, incorporating these checks into routine field inspections.

monitoring independent of individual discretion.

and modification reviews.

structured cross-functional reviews.

to optimize organizational preventive measures.

validating that replacements or upgrades address all known failure modes.

beyond indicator readings—in particular, confirming actuator movements visually during testing.
• Revise operational procedures to guarantee checks and measurements of interface levels in storage tanks prior 
to recirculation or discharge operations, preventing unintentional product releases.

failure does not result in environmental incidents.

A significant release of flammable gas occurred in a subsea production system when the small-diameter pipe 
responsible for chemical injection instrumentation failed completely. The incident went initially unnoticed by 
automatic safety systems. The escape of gas was eventually discovered during scheduled activities using remotely 
operated equipment for another purpose. The event resulted in a discharge of a large volume of gas into the sea; no 
injuries or direct material impact were reported.
WHAT WENT WRONG?
The root cause of the incident was mechanical fatigue of the chemical injection tubing, caused by vibration 
induced by gas flow over time. At the design stage, there were no requirements or practices for assessing the risk 
of vibration on such instrumentation lines attached to the pressure containment body. As a result, the primary 
containment barrier for the chemical injection line failed due to degradation from vibration in a so-called “dead leg” 
configuration. Contributing to the incident, the automated safety and shutdown systems did not detect the event: the 
variation in operational pressure was too small to trigger shutoff actions. The shutdown was performed manually 
after detection.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS & RECOMMENDATIONS:
This incident demonstrates the importance of systematically managing vibration risks in all pressurized 
instrumented lines, including those not traditionally subject to such analysis. It highlights the necessity to embed 
vibration assessment requirements in the technical specifications and project phases for new and existing 
installations. Strengthening the design and verification process helps to ensure the integrity of barriers and timely 
detection of degradation mechanisms that automated process systems may not catch.
Key recommendations derived from the case include:
• Review and update technical requirements for new projects so that analysis for vibration effects, including 
acoustic and flow-induced vibration, is explicitly required for all instrumented lines attached to the main process 
body.
• For systems currently under construction, ensure that vibration studies are extended to cover these instrument 
tubing lines before commissioning.
• For systems already in operation, develop engineering improvements and plan the implementation to ensure 
that all elements subject to comparable service conditions are covered for integrity over their life cycle.
• Calibrate and implement analytical tools to be capable of estimating the time to failure due to vibration fatigue in 
small-bore instrument lines.
• Based on these studies, create specific action plans for each affected facility, including possible reduction of 
operating parameters, scheduled removals, or engineering retrofits needed to guarantee long-term reliability.

standards, practical procedures that are clearly defined and executable, and that relying solely on administrative 
controls is inadequate. The organization must ensure that risk assessments and planning encompass real 
working conditions and that exposure to hazardous situations is controlled by robust physical, engineering, and 
organizational safeguards rather than individual choices.

during planning, documented and implemented in execution.

lacked clear instructions for properly evaluating small-diameter valves, which made the detection of advanced

double isolation mechanism, allowing gas to pass through manual valves and consequently increasing the volume 
released.

accessories, especially small-diameter valves and those involving dissimilar materials. It reinforced the need for 
robust procedures, quality control, and adherence to engineering best practices across similar operations.

• Revise technical specifications and procedures to ensure they address risks associated with dissimilar 
materials.
• Conduct technical workshops for inspection teams on failure mechanisms in small-diameter valves (mainly 
dissimilar materials).

galvanic corrosion.

FUNCTION: Production
CAUSE: Explosion, fire or burns
ACTIVITY: Maintenance, inspection, testing
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Energy isolation
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
On May 20, 2025, a worker was engaged in repositioning a spec blind from the closed to the open position on the 
flare line, in preparation to de-isolate the unit for commissioning activities. During this activity, the worker was 
exposed to a gas/energy release from the down steam side of the isolated gate valve at the open flange pair. Worker 
required rescue from heights and was provided onsite first aid; worker was transported to a local hospital for 
further medical assessment where it was determined worker sustained bruised ribs and a concussion. Worker was 
released from hospital the same day.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
The 10” gate valve used as a single isolation was not fully closed because the chain operator seized due to physical 
interference, giving a false indication that the valve was seated. Pressure verification showed 0 kPag, but this was 
ambiguous because the flare system was under slight vacuum, meaning zero pressure did not confirm positive 
isolation. Oxygen entered the flare piping system through the partially open valve while the flare remained lit,

creating conditions for ignition. When work was performed on the spectacle blind, this led to a deflagration and an 
uncontrolled release of energy that injured the worker.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. Zero pressure does not equal positive isolation - Pressure indication alone is an insufficient barrier for verifying 
isolation in flare systems, especially where vacuum conditions can exist. 
2. Single isolation is not a robust barrier for breaking containment - Single isolation provides little tolerance for 
hidden failures and should not be relied upon where severe energy release is credible. 
3. Equipment condition and work environment directly shape human decision-making - People act on the cues the 
system gives them; degraded equipment and obstructed layouts can actively mislead competent workers. 
4. Permits and risk classification must reflect real hazard potential - Administrative controls lose credibility when 
they do not reflect the true severity of the hazard.

AFRICA OFFSHORE
DATE: 07 Jul 2025
COUNTRY: Ghana
FUNCTION: Production
CAUSE: Pressure release
ACTIVITY: Production operations
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
On 7th July 2025 at 15:03 hrs, a hydrocarbon gas release occurred onboard the FPSO from anti-surge valve (part 
of the gas compression system). Gas detectors were activated and an Emergency Shutdown Level 2 (ESD-2) was 
triggered, resulting in a full production shutdown. The Emergency Response Team confirmed stem leakage on the 
anti-surge valve.
The valve was isolated and inspected. Only remnants of stem packing were found. A temporary in-situ repair 
was attempted using graphite split and braided rings, but the installation sequence was incorrect. The valve was 
therefore not leak-tested and sent onshore for further assessment.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
Critical Factor 1: Stem packing was not checked after approximately 500 strokes for load and re-tightened. If this 
had been done the valve stem leak would not have occurred in the opinion of the investigation team.
Critical Factor 2: None of the documentation provided with the valve identified the requirement to recheck the 
tightness of the packing as prescribed at approximately 500 strokes of the valve. The valve assembly drawing lacked 
detailed information, particularly regarding the installation sequence of the packing types and the lantern ring (a 
spacer within the packing arrangement).
Critical Factor 3: In conjunction with the lack of details within the drawing available, the IM (Inventory Management) 
numbers used in the Company system did not fully address the requirements of the valve stem packing 
requirements.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. PV-2030A-02 was sent onshore for an RCA. Evidence found support the root cause of the leak as described above.
2. The stem packing has been dismantled and rebuilt at contractor facility, who obtained the detailed drawing for 
packing installation sequence and components. The valve was tested with nitrogen at 373barg whilst submerged in 
a water bath to prove leak tight. The valve was stroked during this test. The valve is now back in service.
3. Ongoing inspection of all actuated valves in gas service to identify any weeps/leaks. FLIR camera is using infra 
red technology to identify any hydrocarbon releases to atmosphere.
• FV in gas export service was remediated by the offshore team
• There was also another valve within the weep register, PV-2020-05 which started to leak on 13th August. It has 
been isolated to stop the atmospheric release as this valve is not required during normal operation.
• No other valves identified with weeps or leaks.

installation requirements, particularly for sensitive or delicate instrumentation.

includes defined replacement criteria and condition assessments based on operational exposure, rather than time-
based intervals alone.

DATE: 08 Apr 2025
COUNTRY: Qatar
FUNCTION: Production
CAUSE: Pressure release
ACTIVITY: Maintenance, inspection, testing
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Energy isolation
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
A contractor mechanical field service representative and mechanical team had disconnected the export gas 
compressor gas turbine’s primary and secondary flexible fuel gas hoses. After disconnecting the hoses, the 
contractor field service representative was on the back side of the gas turbine while the mechanical technicians 
were on the front side. While lying beneath the gas turbine to check the water wash drain tube under the gas 
turbine, pressure was released, causing the loose hoses to swing.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
One of the loose hoses struck the helmet of the mechanical field service representative, resulting in physical 
damage to the helmet.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Trapped pressure must always be safely discharged before disconnecting components, even when the system 
appears isolated - especially in high-pressure gas systems.
• Contractor activities must be fully integrated into company isolation procedures, including proper 
documentation in Process Isolation Certificates, to avoid oversight of critical steps.
• Safe Work Method Statements (SWMS) must include detailed, step-by-step instructions, particularly for non-
routine tasks, to ensure consistent understanding and execution.
• Non-routine activities require Task Risk Assessments (TRA) regardless of pressure levels or perceived risk, as 
they often involve unexpected hazards.
• System manipulations (e.g., Programmable Logic Controller forcing) must not occur without coordination and 
approval from the Area Authority, and only after confirming all personnel are in safe positions.

testing regulators before leaving the test stand and putting the pump into service.
E-Tech manager will provide a procedure for the established gas train and the testing procedure in an SOP for 
running gas including all hookup and parts that are approved.
